Pour la première fois en France, son organisateur, le commissaire d'exposition Jean-Hubert Martin, a placé sur la scène internationale de l'art contemporain les arts « non occidentaux » contemporains.

text: Lille (Rijsel en néerlandais, Rysel en flamand, Lile en picard), est une ville du Nord de la France. Préfecture du département du Nord et chef-lieu de la région Hauts-de-France, elle est le siège de l'Autorité douanière de l'Union Européenne.

title: élections européennes ; succès de la liste RPR-UDF de Valéry Giscard d'Estaing.
text: Valéry Giscard d'Estaing, communément appelé « Giscard » et également connu sous ses initiales VGE, né le 2 février 1926 à Coblence (Allemagne) et mort le 2 décembre 2020 à Authon (Loir-et-Cher), est un homme d'État français. Il est président de la République française du 27 mai 1974 au 21 mai 1981.

title: loi Bambuck contre le dopage sportif.
text: Roger Bambuck, né le 22 novembre 1945 à Pointe-à-Pitre, est un athlète français spécialiste des épreuves de sprint. Il est considéré comme l'un des meilleurs sprinteurs français, en étant le seul à avoir détenu le record du monde du 100 m et en ayant réalisé la meilleure performance française dans cette discipline aux Jeux olympiques.

text: En France, les instituts universitaires de formation des maîtres sont, de 1990 à 2013 (2015 en Nouvelle-Calédonie), des établissements de formation des professionnels de l'enseignement public (professeurs des premier et second degrés, conseillers principaux d'éducation). title: loi no 89-470 approuvant le Xe Plan de développement économique et social. Mise en place des contrats de ville.
text: Le contrat de ville permet de réaliser des projets urbains sous la forme contractuelle entre l'État, les collectivités locales et leurs partenaires. Il a été créé par la loi du 10 juillet 1989 approuvant le Xe plan afin d'intervenir sur l'habitat, l'environnement, l'éducation, les transports, la sécurité, la culture, les équipements sportifs, ou les services sociaux.

title: loi instituant le permis à points.
text: Le permis de conduire est un droit administratif donnant autorisation de conduire certains véhicules motorisés tels qu'automobile, motocyclette, cyclomoteur, camion ou autobus, dans un ensemble de pays. La délivrance du permis de conduire peut être soumise selon les cas et les lois locales à un test d'aptitude à la conduite de niveau de difficulté variable ainsi qu'à des exigences d'âge minimal.

title: inauguration de l’opéra Bastille à Paris.
text: L'opéra Bastille est une salle d'opéra moderne située sur la place de la Bastille à Paris. Elle est conçue par Carlos Ott et inaugurée en 1989 à l'occasion des festivités du bicentenaire de la Révolution dans le cadre des grands travaux pour Paris.

title: ouverture des cérémonies du bicentenaire de la Révolution française ; « La Marseillaise », défilé sur les Champs-Élysées orchestré par Jean-Paul Goude.
text: Le bicentenaire de la Révolution est un évènement commémoratif organisé en 1989, principalement en France, pour la célébration du 200e anniversaire de la Révolution française, et plus particulièrement de la prise de la Bastille le 14 juillet 1789, et de la Déclaration des droits de l'homme et du citoyen le 26 août 1789. Ce jubilé a été l'occasion d'analyser les différentes interprétations de ce phénomène révolutio…

title: 14-16 juillet : sommet de l’Arche, réunion du G7 à La Défense.
text: Le sommet du G7 de 1989, 15e réunion du G7, réunit les dirigeants des 7 pays démocratiques les plus industrialisés, ou G7, du 14 au 16 juillet 1989, dans le quartier d'affaires français de La Défense.

title: inauguration de l’Arche de la Défense.
text: L’arche de la Défense ou Grande Arche est un édifice monumental situé dans le quartier d'affaires de La Défense à l'ouest de Paris, sur le territoire de la commune de Puteaux. Son inauguration s'est tenue le 14 juillet 1989, au moment du bicentenaire de la Révolution sous le nom de « grande arche de la Fraternité ».

title: affaire des paras de Francazal. Deux appelés déserteurs, Thierry El Borgi et Philippe Siauve, sont arrêtés à l'issue d'une série de meurtres et de viols commis depuis le 30 mai dans la région de Toulouse.
text: L'affaire des paras de Francazal est une affaire criminelle française dans laquelle quatre appelés parachutistes déserteurs du camp militaire logistique situé près de la base aérienne 101 Toulouse-Francazal, appartenant à l'arme du Matériel, ont tué une femme et deux adolescentes ainsi qu'un garde-chasse en 1989. title: attentat contre un DC-10 français d’UTA qui explose au-dessus du Niger, faisant 170 morts.
text: Le vol UTA 772 est un vol international régulier reliant Brazzaville, en république du Congo, à Paris, en France, avec une escale prévue à N'Djaména, au Tchad. Le 19 septembre 1989, le McDonnell Douglas DC-10 assurant ce vol est victime d'un attentat à la bombe : l'avion explose au-dessus du désert du Ténéré, près de Bilma au Niger, tuant les 170 passagers et membres d'équipage.

text: Salzgitter AG is a German company, one of the largest steel producers in Europe with an annual output of around seven million tonnes. With over 100 subsidiaries and associated companies, the Group is structured in four business units – Steel Production, Steel Processing, Trading and Technology – under the umbrella of a management holding company.

title: Prime Minister Ranasinghe Premadasa takes office as the third President of Sri Lanka.
text: Sri Lankabhimanya Ranasinghe Premadasa was a Sri Lankan politician who served as the third president of Sri Lanka from 1989 until his assassination in 1993. A longtime member of the United National Party, he previously served as Prime Minister of Sri Lanka from 1978 to 1989, with his tenure making him the longest-serving uninterrupted Prime Minister of Sri Lanka.

title: Gulf of Sidra incident (1989): Two Libyan MiG-23 "Floggers" are engaged and shot down by two US Navy F-14 Tomcats.
text: On 4 January 1989, two Grumman F-14A Tomcats of the United States Navy shot down two Libyan-operated Mikoyan-Gurevich MiG-23ML Flogger-G which the American aircrews believed were attempting to engage and attack them, as had happened eight years prior during the 1981 Gulf of Sidra incident. The engagement took place over the Mediterranean Sea, about 40 miles north of Tobruk, Libya.

title: Emperor Hirohito dies; his son Akihito ascends as the 125th Emperor of Japan, followed by the change in the era name from Shōwa to Heisei on the following day.
text: Hirohito, also known by his posthumous name Emperor Shōwa, was Emperor of Japan from 25 December 1926 until his death in 1989. He is the longest-reigning non-legendary emperor in Japanese history and one of the longest-reigning monarchs in the world.

title: British Midland Flight 092 (a Boeing 737-400) crashes on an M1 motorway near the East Midlands Airport, 47 people were killed and 79 people survived.
text: The Kegworth air disaster occurred when British Midland Airways Flight 092, a Boeing 737-400, crashed onto the motorway embankment between the M1 motorway and A453 road near Kegworth, Leicestershire, England, while attempting to make an emergency landing at East Midlands Airport on 8 January 1989. The aircraft was on a scheduled flight from London Heathrow Airport to Belfast International Airport.

title: In accordance with United Nations Security Council Resolution 626 and the New York Accords, Cuban troops begin withdrawing from Angola.
text: United Nations Security Council resolution 626, adopted unanimously on 20 December 1988, after noting an agreement between Angola and Cuba regarding the withdrawal of Cuban troops from Angola and considering a report by the Secretary-General, the Council endorsed the report and established the United Nations Angola Verification Mission I for a period of thirty-one months. The Council decided the mission would ente…

title: The Lexus and Infiniti luxury car brands are launched at the North American International Auto Show in Detroit with the unveiling of the 1990 Lexus LS and Infiniti Q45 sedans.
text: The Lexus LS is a series of full-size luxury sedans that have served as the flagship model of Lexus, the luxury division of Toyota, since 1989. For the first four generations, all LS models featured V8 engines and were predominantly rear-wheel-drive.

title: Former Ugandan dictator Idi Amin is expelled to Senegal from Zaire after using a fake Zairean passport in an attempt to return to Uganda. Amin is eventually expelled from Senegal and subsequently returns to Zaire after the Saudi government…
text: Awon'go Idi Amin Dada Oumee was a Ugandan military officer and dictator who served as the third president of Uganda from 1971 until his overthrow in 1979. He gained power after the 1971 Ugandan coup d'état and subsequently ruled the country under a regime characterized by rampant human rights abuses, economic mismanagement and corruption.

title: Thirty-five European nations, meeting in Vienna, agree to strengthen human rights and improve East–West trade.
text: Human rights are moral principles or norms that establish standards of human behavior and are often protected by both national and international laws. These rights are considered inherent and inalienable, meaning they belong to every individual simply by virtue of being human.

title: Ante Marković succeeds Branko Mikulić as Prime Minister of Yugoslavia.
text: Ante Marković was a Yugoslav politician, businessman and engineer. He is most notable for having served as the last Prime Minister of Yugoslavia from 1989 to 1991.

title: George H. W. Bush is inaugurated as President of the United States.
text: George Herbert Walker Bush was the 41st president of the United States, serving from 1989 to 1993. A member of the Republican Party, he served as the 43rd vice president under Ronald Reagan and previously held a multitude of other federal, ambassadorial, and party positions.

title: January 23–24 – Armed civilian leftists briefly attack and occupy an Argentinian army base near Buenos Aires.
text: The 1989 Attack on La Tablada barracks also known as the Battle of La Tablada occurred on 23 and 24 January 1989 when 40 members of Movimiento Todos por la Patria attacked the military barracks in La Tablada, in Buenos Aires Province, Argentina. 39 people were killed and 60 injured by the time the Argentine army retook the barracks.

title: The two longest-imprisoned German WWII war criminals in Western Europe, Ferdinand aus der Fünten and Franz Fischer (collectively known as The Breda Two), were released from Dutch prison.
text: Ferdinand Hugo aus der Fünten, widely known as Fünten, was an SS-Hauptsturmführer and head of the Central Office for Jewish Emigration in Amsterdam during the Second World War. He was responsible for the deportation of Jews from the Netherlands to the German concentration camps and was convicted as a war criminal.

title: Prime Minister of Canada Brian Mulroney shuffles his cabinet, appointing six new ministers and reassigning the responsibilities of nineteen others.
text: The prime minister of Canada is the head of government of Canada. Under the Westminster system, the prime minister governs with the confidence of a majority of the elected House of Commons; as such, the prime minister typically sits as a member of Parliament and leads the largest party or a coalition of parties.

title: U.S. President Bush meets Canadian Prime Minister Brian Mulroney in Ottawa, laying the groundwork for the Acid Rain Treaty of 1991.
text: Martin Brian Mulroney was a Canadian lawyer, businessman, and politician who served as the 18th prime minister of Canada from 1984 to 1993. He led the Progressive Conservative Party of Canada and served as a member of Parliament (MP) from 1983 to 1993.

title: The Arab Maghreb Union (AMU) is formed.
text: The Arab Maghreb Union is a political union and economic union trade agreement aiming for economic and future political unity among Arab countries that are located primarily in the Maghreb in North Africa. Its members are the nations of Algeria, Libya, Mauritania, Morocco and Tunisia.

title: South African police raid the home of Winnie Mandela and arrest four of her bodyguards.
text: Nomzamo Winifred Zanyiwe Madikizela-Mandela, also known as Winnie Mandela, was a South African politician and anti-apartheid activist who was the second wife of Nelson Mandela. During her political career, she served as a Member of Parliament from 1994 to 2003, and from 2009 until her death, and was a deputy minister of arts and culture from 1994 to 1996.

title: In Canada's Yukon Territory, the ruling New Democrats narrowly maintain control of the Yukon Legislative Assembly, winning 9 seats vs. the Progressive Conservative Party's 7.
text: The Yukon Legislative Assembly is the legislative assembly for Yukon, Canada. Unique among Canada's three territories, the Yukon Legislative Assembly is the only territorial legislature which is organized along political party lines.

title: After protracted testimony, the U.S. Senate Armed Services Committee rejects, 11–9, President Bush's nomination of John Tower for Secretary of Defense.
text: John Goodwin Tower was an American politician and military veteran who represented Texas in the United States Senate from 1961 to 1985. He was the first Republican elected to the U.S. Senate from Texas since Reconstruction.

title: The state funeral of Emperor Shōwa (Hirohito) in Tokyo is attended by leaders and representatives of 160 nations.
text: A state funeral is a public funeral ceremony, observing the strict rules of protocol, held to honour people of national significance. State funerals often include much pomp and ceremony as well as religious overtones and distinctive elements of military tradition.

title: The Satanic Verses controversy: Iran places a $3,000,000 bounty on the head of The Satanic Verses author Salman Rushdie.
text: Sir Ahmed Salman Rushdie is an Indian-born British and American novelist. His work often combines magical realism with historical fiction and primarily deals with connections, disruptions, and migrations between Eastern and Western civilizations.

title: Singing Revolution: After 44 years, the Estonian flag is raised at the Pikk Hermann tower in Tallinn.
text: The Singing Revolution was a series of events from 1987 to 1991 that led to the restoration of independence of the three Soviet-occupied Baltic countries of Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania at the end of the Cold War. The Soviet Union annexed the Baltics around 1940, following the Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact, though this annexation was not widely recognized.
